A HIPAA-enabled app must have auto log-off. If a user is inactive for a certain amount of time, the system should log them out to protect sensitive health data and prevent unauthorized access.

import android.app.Application
import android.content.Context
import android.content.Intent
import android.os.Handler
import android.os.Looper
import androidx.lifecycle.DefaultLifecycleObserver
import androidx.lifecycle.LifecycleOwner
import androidx.lifecycle.ProcessLifecycleOwner

object AutoLogoutManager : DefaultLifecycleObserver {
    private const val TIMEOUT_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000L // 5 minutes
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
    private lateinit var appContext: Context

    private val timeoutRunnable = Runnable { performLogout() }

    fun init(app: Application) {
        appContext = app.applicationContext
        ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.addObserver(this)
        resetTimer() // start counting as soon as app is foregrounded
    }

    fun onUserInteraction() = resetTimer()

    private fun resetTimer() {
        handler.removeCallbacks(timeoutRunnable)
        handler.postDelayed(timeoutRunnable, TIMEOUT_MS)
    }

    override fun onStart(owner: LifecycleOwner) {
        // App came to foreground → (re)start inactivity timer
        resetTimer()
    }

    override fun onStop(owner: LifecycleOwner) {
        // App went to background → optionally log out immediately OR shorten timer
        // performLogout() // Uncomment if you want instant lock on background
    }

    private fun performLogout() {
        // 1) Clear auth/session (example with SharedPreferences)
        val prefs = appContext.getSharedPreferences("auth", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
        prefs.edit().remove("access_token").apply()

        // 2) Navigate to Login and clear back stack
        val intent = Intent(appContext, LoginActivity::class.java).apply {
            addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK)
        }
        appContext.startActivity(intent)
    }
}

U.S. Department of Health & Human Services. (2013). Security Standards: Technical Safeguards §164.312(a)(2)(iii) Automatic Logoff. 45 C.F.R. §164.312. Retrieved from https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164

In HIPAA, encryption protects patient data by making it unreadable to unauthorized users, while decryption ensures only authorized access. This safeguards PHI, prevents misuse in breaches, and ensures compliance with HIPAA’s Security Rule.

In rails version 7.0 to 8, Follow the steps and follow the official guide at https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_record_encryption.html:
Step 1: Run bin/rails db:encryption:init to generate a random key set:

$ bin/rails db:encryption:init
Add this entry to the credentials of the target environment:

active_record_encryption:
  primary_key: EGY8WhulUOXixybod7ZWwMIL68R9o5kC
  deterministic_key: aPA5XyALhf75NNnMzaspW7akTfZp0lPY
  key_derivation_salt: xEY0dt6TZcAMg52K7O84wYzkjvbA62Hz

Step 2: In your model, specify which columns to encrypts 
class User < ApplicationRecord

end

Step 3: Simply create your ActiveRecord object as follows:

If you're using an ORM like ActiveRecord or Sequel, using attr_encrypted is easy:

  class User
    attr_encrypted :ssn, key: 'your 256 bits key'
  end


  user = User.new

  user.ssn # returns the unencrypted object ie. '123-45-6789'
  user.encrypted_ssn # returns the encrypted version of :ssn

Using cancancan gem 
# app/models/ability.rb
class Ability
  include CanCan::Ability

  def initialize(user)
    # Least privilege: a user can read/update ONLY their own patient row
    can [:read, :update], Patient, user_id: user.id
  end
end

# app/models/patient.rb
class Patient < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :user  # owner of the record
end

# app/controllers/patients_controller.rb
class PatientsController < ApplicationController
  before_action :authenticate_user!
  load_and_authorize_resource  # loads @patient/@patients & checks permission for each action

  def show
    # @patient already loaded & authorized
  end

  def index
    # @patients already scoped to what current_user can read
    # (equivalent to Patient.accessible_by(current_ability))
  end

  def update
    if @patient.update(patient_params)
      redirect_to @patient, notice: "Updated"
    else
      render :edit, status: :unprocessable_entity
    end
  end

  private

  def patient_params
    params.require(:patient).permit(:first_name, :last_name, :dob)
  end
end

An unsafe HostnameVerifier implementation in an Android application is an implementation that does not properly verify the hostname of the server with which the application is communicating. This can allow an attacker to impersonate a legitimate server and trick the application into sending sensitive data to the attacker.

Most apps should just use the default verifier (no custom code). If you must restrict to a single hostname, scope it to that client and delegate to the default: 
val strictVerifier = javax.net.ssl.HostnameVerifier { hostname, session ->
    if (!"api.healthCareSite.com".equals(hostname, ignoreCase = true)) return@HostnameVerifier false
    javax.net.ssl.HttpsURLConnection.getDefaultHostnameVerifier().verify(hostname, session)
}

val client = okhttp3.OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .hostnameVerifier(strictVerifier)           // ← scoped to THIS OkHttpClient
    .build()

Mechanisms to corroborate that PHI has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner

This HIPAA rule may be ensured using cancancan gem as follows: 
# app/controllers/patient_records_controller.rb
class PatientRecordsController < ApplicationController
  load_and_authorize_resource

  rescue_from CanCan::AccessDenied do
    render json: { error: "Not authorized" }, status: :forbidden
  end
  def update
    authorize! :update, @patient
    @patient = Patient.find(params[:id])
    @patient.update(patient_params)
  end
  def destroy
    authorize! :destroy, @patient
    @patient = Patient.find(params[:id])
    @patient.destroy
  end
end

This controller action ensures that only authorized users can update or destroy patient record. It uses CanCanCan’s load_and_authorize_resource to automatically check permissions, and the authorize! :update and authorize! :destroy, @patient object makes sure the current user has the right to update or destroy the requested patient. If someone without permission tries to update or destroy it, the rescue_from block returns a 403 response with a clear “Not authorized” message.

https://github.com/CanCanCommunity/cancancan

code_snippet:
This HIPAA rule can be implemented using Rails Devise gem and JWT ruby library. One of the examples could be as follows:

module AuthApi
  class JsonWebToken
    class << self
      def encode(payload, exp = 24.hours.from_now)
        payload[:exp] = exp.to_i
        JWT.encode(payload, Rails.application.secrets.secret_key_base)
      end

      def decode(token)
        body = JWT.decode(token, Rails.application.secrets.secret_key_base)[0]
        HashWithIndifferentAccess.new body
      rescue
        nil
      end
    end
  end
  class AuthorizeApiRequest
    def initialize(headers = {})
      @headers = headers
    end

    def call
      JsonWebToken.decode(extract_token_from_auth_header)
    end

    def valid_token?(token)
      Devise.secure_compare(token, extract_token_from_auth_header)
    end

    private
    attr_reader :headers

    def extract_token_from_auth_header
      if headers['Authorization'].present?
        headers['Authorization'].split(' ').last
      else
        raise 'Authorization Error.'
      end
    end
  end
end


class ApiController < ActionController::Base

  protect_from_forgery with: :null_session
  before_action :authenticate_user_from_jwt!

  #rescue_from StandardError, with: :render_500

  private

  def render_500(e)
    puts e.message
    puts e.backtrace
    render json: { errors: ["Internal Server Error"] }, status: :internal_server_error
  end

  def authenticate_user_from_jwt!
    new_api_request = AuthApi::AuthorizeApiRequest.new(request.headers)
    user_hash = new_api_request.call
    user = User.find_by(email: user_hash[:email]) if user_hash.present?
    if user && new_api_request.valid_token?(user.jwt_token)
      sign_in user, store: false
    else
      head :unauthorized
    end
  end

end

    if user && user.valid_password?(params[:password])
      token = AuthApi::JsonWebToken.encode({ email: user.email })
      user.update_attribute(:jwt_token, token)
      render json: user.to_json(only: [:name, :email, :first_name, :last_name, :jwt_token])
    else
      render json: {errors: ["Email or password is invalid!"]}, status: :unauthorized
    end
  end

Add multi-factor authentication to your Android app


Signing users in with a second factor

To sign in a user with two-factor SMS verification:
  1. Sign the user in with their first factor, then catch the FirebaseAuthMultiFactorException exception. This error contains a resolver, which you can use to obtain the user's enrolled second factors. It also contains an underlying session proving the user successfully authenticated with their first factor. For example, if the user's first factor was an email and password:
FirebaseAuth.getInstance()
    .signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password)
    .addOnCompleteListener(
        OnCompleteListener { task ->
            if (task.isSuccessful) {
                // User is not enrolled with a second factor and is successfully
                // signed in.
                // ...
                return@OnCompleteListener
            }
            if (task.exception is FirebaseAuthMultiFactorException) {
                // The user is a multi-factor user. Second factor challenge is
                // required.
                val multiFactorResolver =
                    (task.exception as FirebaseAuthMultiFactorException).resolver
                // ...
            } else {
                // Handle other errors, such as wrong password.
            }
        })
If the user's first factor is a federated provider, such as OAuth, catch the error after calling startActivityForSignInWithProvider().

2. If the user has multiple secondary factors enrolled, ask them which one to use:
// Ask user which second factor to use.
// You can get the list of enrolled second factors using
//   multiFactorResolver.hints

// Check the selected factor:
if (multiFactorResolver.hints[selectedIndex].factorId
    === PhoneMultiFactorGenerator.FACTOR_ID
) {
    // User selected a phone second factor.
    val selectedHint =
        multiFactorResolver.hints[selectedIndex] as PhoneMultiFactorInfo
} else if (multiFactorResolver.hints[selectedIndex].factorId
    === TotpMultiFactorGenerator.FACTOR_ID) {
    // User selected a TOTP second factor.
} else {
    // Unsupported second factor.
}

Normally, web server like Apache or Nginx ensures this by integrating ssl certificate and use Rails as backend which run on http on port 3000. But still the Rails application must set config.force_ssl = true in production mode.

So you can achieve this rule in web server side. As an example, here is an implementation below:
# :80 => :443 redirect
<VirtualHost *:80>
  ServerName example.com
  RewriteEngine On
  RewriteRule ^ https://%{HTTP_HOST}%{REQUEST_URI} [R=301,L]
</VirtualHost>

# HTTPS vhost
<VirtualHost *:443>
  ServerName example.com

  SSLEngine on
  SSLCertificateFile /path/fullchain.pem
  SSLCertificateKeyFile /path/privkey.pem
  # Strong TLS (adjust to your policy)
  SSLProtocol             all -SSLv3 -TLSv1 -TLSv1.1
  SSLCipherSuite          HIGH:!aNULL:!MD5
  SSLHonorCipherOrder     on
  SSLCompression          off
  Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload"

  # Keep original Host (important for URL helpers in Rails)
  ProxyPreserveHost On

  # Forward scheme/port so Rails sees HTTPS
  RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Proto "https"
  RequestHeader set X-Forwarded-Port  "443"

  # Forward client IP (optional but recommended)
  # Requires mod_remoteip; also set RemoteIPInternalProxy to your proxy’s IP(s)
  RemoteIPHeader X-Forwarded-For
  RemoteIPInternalProxy 127.0.0.1

  # Proxy to Rails on :3000 (HTTP upstream)
  ProxyPass        / http://127.0.0.1:3000/
  ProxyPassReverse / http://127.0.0.1:3000/
</VirtualHost>


However, in Rails you can make sure https is on as follows:

Enforces HTTPS correctly (confidentiality + integrity) 
# config/environments/production.rb
config.force_ssl = true
# Enables HSTS (includes subdomains + long max-age)
config.ssl_options = {
  hsts: { expires: 1.year, subdomains: true, preload: true }

Android's AppOpsManager API enables comprehensive monitoring of all private data access operations — including those performed by third-party libraries. The following reference implementation captures the authenticated user identity, operation type, and timestamp for each data access event, and persists audit records to a secure local database for compliance review.

Code Example:
private void logPrivateDataAccess(
        String opCode, String trace) {
    auditRepository.insert(new AuditRecord( // persist audit record in database (not just logging)
        getCurrentAuthenticatedUser(), // identifies which authenticated user accessed private data
        opCode, // type of private data accessed (e.g., location, contacts, camera, microphone)
        Instant.now().toString(),
        trace // where the private data access happened in code
    ));
}
// Register in onCreate()
AppOpsManager appOps =
        getSystemService(AppOpsManager.class);
appOps.setOnOpNotedCallback(getMainExecutor(),
    new AppOpsManager.OnOpNotedCallback() {
        @Override public void onNoted(SyncNotedAppOp op) { // called when app accesses private data synchronously
            logPrivateDataAccess(op.getOp(), // private data access operation
                Arrays.toString(
                    new Throwable().getStackTrace()));
        }
        @Override public void onSelfNoted(SyncNotedAppOp op) { // called when app itself initiates private data access
            logPrivateDataAccess(op.getOp(), // private data access operation
                Arrays.toString(
                    new Throwable().getStackTrace()));
        }
        @Override public void onAsyncNoted(AsyncNotedAppOp op) { // called when private data is accessed asynchronously (background)
            logPrivateDataAccess(
                op.getOp(), // private data access operation
                op.getMessage());
        }
    });

A well-designed app should use optimal, deny-by-default authorization with fail-safe handling to prevent broken access control. That aligns with OWASP guidance to centralize authorization checks, enforce least privilege, and default to secure outcomes—key to improving your scanner’s score and keeping the app HIPAA-ready.


Step 1 — Define a domain AuthorizationException and a strict guard

Why: App/business-rule authorization should fail closed with a clear, catchable signal—don’t “fix up” failed checks. This is standard secure-design / OWASP practice (deny by default + fail-safe). 


class AuthorizationException(message: String) : RuntimeException(message)

fun authorizeOrThrow(user: UserCtx, res: Resource, action: String) {
    val allowed = when (action) {
        "read"   -> "res:read" in user.scopes || "ROLE_ADMIN" in user.roles
        "update" -> "res:write" in user.scopes || "ROLE_ADMIN" in user.roles
        else     -> false
    }
    if (!allowed) throw AuthorizationException("Denied: action=$action on kind=${res.kind}")
}


Step 2 — Avoid reflection for sensitive data; handle IllegalAccessException

Why: Java/Kotlin throw IllegalAccessException when reflective code touches members it isn’t allowed to access—don’t use reflection to “peek” at protected data, and if it’s unavoidable, catch and fail safely. Source

class SecretStore { private val secretToken: String = "TOP-SECRET-DEMO" }

fun readSecretReflectively(): String {
    val store = SecretStore()
    val field = SecretStore::class.java.getDeclaredField("secretToken")
    return try {
        // No setAccessible(true) → should throw
        field.get(store) as String
    } catch (ex: IllegalAccessException) {
        println("CATCH:IllegalAccessException msg='${ex::class.simpleName}'")
        "REDACTED"
    }
}
Developer integration:
  • If a library uses reflection under the hood, wrap the call, catch IllegalAccessException, and do not leak data in logs or messages.


Step 3 — Where this fits on Android and server code
  • Android: Platform permission/policy failures surface as SecurityException (e.g., missing dangerous permission, restricted API). Handle the errors, and never include PHI in messages. Android Developers

try {
    authorizeOrThrow(currentUser, resource, "update")
    // ... perform action ...
} catch (e: AuthorizationException) {
    // Map to 403 / UX error, log without PHI
} catch (e: SecurityException) {
    // Platform/permission failure — prompt for permission or abort safely
}

Centralize Authentication & Protect Credentials: Use Spring Security’s AuthenticationManager (or AuthenticationProvider) to authenticate, with a strong PasswordEncoder (e.g., BCrypt). Do not pass identities via request parameters for authorization, never log credentials, and return uniform failure messages to avoid user enumeration. Prefer token/OIDC for stateless APIs.
// Security config: AuthenticationManager + BCrypt
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
class SecurityConfig {

  @Bean
  public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable()); // for pure API; keep enabled for form flows
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/auth/**").permitAll()
        .anyRequest().authenticated());
    return http.build();
  }

  @Bean
  public PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  // If using a custom UserDetailsService:
  @Bean
  public AuthenticationManager authManager(HttpSecurity http, PasswordEncoder pw,
                                           UserDetailsService uds) throws Exception {
    return http.getSharedObject(AuthenticationManagerBuilder.class)
               .userDetailsService(uds).passwordEncoder(pw)
               .and().build();
  }
}


// Controller: authenticate via AuthenticationManager (no credential logging)
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/auth")
class AuthController {

  private final AuthenticationManager authManager;
  private final TokenService tokenService; // your JWT/Opaque token service

  AuthController(AuthenticationManager authManager, TokenService tokenService) {
    this.authManager = authManager;
    this.tokenService = tokenService;
  }

  @PostMapping("/login")
  public ResponseEntity<?> login(@RequestBody LoginRequest req) {
    // NEVER log req.getPassword(); avoid printing the username on failure
    var authReq = new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(req.getUsername(), req.getPassword());
    try {
      var auth = authManager.authenticate(authReq);        // <-- .authenticate(...)
      SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth);
      String token = tokenService.issue(auth);             // JWT or opaque token
      return ResponseEntity.ok(new TokenResponse(token));
    } catch (AuthenticationException ex) {
      // Uniform error (no user-enumeration hints)
      return ResponseEntity.status(401).body(Map.of("error", "Invalid credentials"));
    }
  }
}

record LoginRequest(String username, String password) {}
record TokenResponse(String accessToken) {}

code_snippet:
Step 1 — Enforce deny-by-default authorization
All requests should be denied unless explicitly permitted. Define granular rules in HttpSecurity or method-level annotations.

@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {
  @Bean
  public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()
        .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
        .anyRequest().authenticated()   // deny by default
    );
    return http.build();
  }
}

Step 2 — Use method-level authorization for business logic
Never rely solely on controller-level or UI-side checks. Enforce authorization in service methods with Spring Security annotations or custom access evaluators.

@Service
public class PatientService {
  @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.name")
  public Patient getPatient(String id) {
    return repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
  }
}
Step 3 — Avoid trusting request parameters for authorization
Never authorize based on request.getParameter() or request.getHeader() values. Always derive identity and roles from the SecurityContextHolder.

Step 4 — Centralize error handling
When access is denied, return a generic 403 response using a custom AccessDeniedHandler. Do not reveal internal roles, resource IDs, or PHI in error messages.

@Component
public class JsonAccessDeniedHandler implements AccessDeniedHandler {
  @Override
  public void handle(HttpServletRequest req,
                     HttpServletResponse res,
                     AccessDeniedException ex) throws IOException {
    res.setStatus(HttpServletResponse.SC_FORBIDDEN);
    res.setContentType("application/json");
    res.getWriter().write("{\"error\":\"Access is denied\"}");
  }
}
Step 5 — Audit denied attempts
Log denied access events with userId, URI, and requestId (but no PHI). Forward these to SIEM or auditing systems for monitoring and compliance reporting.

Step 1 — Enable auditing safely
Annotate your Spring Boot configuration with @EnableJpaAuditing and provide a Clock + DateTimeProvider to enforce UTC.

@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing(dateTimeProviderRef = "utcDateTimeProvider")
public class JpaConfig {
  @Bean
  public DateTimeProvider utcDateTimeProvider(Clock clock) {
    return () -> Optional.of(Instant.now(clock));
  }
  @Bean
  public Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); }
}
Step 2 — Implement a custom AuditorAware
Never hardcode "system". Instead, derive the user from Spring Security’s Authentication.

@Bean
public AuditorAware<String> auditorProvider() {
  return () -> Optional.ofNullable(
    SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()
  ).filter(Authentication::isAuthenticated)
   .map(Authentication::getName)
   .or(() -> Optional.of("system:unknown"));
}
Step 3 — Secure auditing fields
Use @CreatedBy / @CreatedDate with updatable = false. Exclude them from request DTOs and mark as @JsonIgnore if exposed.

@Entity
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public class Patient {
  @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;

  @CreatedDate @Column(nullable=false, updatable=false)
  private Instant createdAt;

  @LastModifiedDate private Instant updatedAt;

  @CreatedBy @Column(nullable=false, updatable=false)
  private String createdBy;

  @LastModifiedBy private String updatedBy;
}
Step 4 — Enforce compliance

  • Encrypt audit tables at rest.

  • Restrict audit-field read access (RBAC).

  • Apply retention policies.

  • Pair with Envers @Audited on critical entities for full history.

  • Keep entity callbacks lightweight and avoid logging PHI.

HttpURLConnection

A URLConnection with support for HTTP-specific features.
   URL url = new URL("http://www.healthSite.com/");
   HttpURLConnection urlConnection = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection();
   try {
     InputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(urlConnection.getInputStream());
     readStream(in);
   } finally {
     urlConnection.disconnect();
   }

By default, this implementation of HttpURLConnection requests that servers use gzip compression and it automatically decompresses the data for callers of URLConnection.getInputStream(). The Content-Encoding and Content-Length response headers are cleared in this case. Gzip compression can be disabled by setting the acceptable encodings in the request header:


   urlConnection.setRequestProperty("Accept-Encoding", "identity");

Setting the Accept-Encoding request header explicitly disables automatic decompression and leaves the response headers intact; callers must handle decompression as needed, according to the Content-Encoding header of the response.

Posting Content
To upload data to a web server, configure the connection for output using setDoOutput(true).
For best performance, you should call either setFixedLengthStreamingMode(int) when the body length is known in advance, or setChunkedStreamingMode(int) when it is not. Otherwise HttpURLConnection will be forced to buffer the complete request body in memory before it is transmitted, wasting (and possibly exhausting) heap and increasing latency.

For example, to perform an upload:
   HttpURLConnection urlConnection = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection();
   try {
     urlConnection.setDoOutput(true);
     urlConnection.setChunkedStreamingMode(0);

     OutputStream out = new BufferedOutputStream(urlConnection.getOutputStream());
     writeStream(out);

     InputStream in = new BufferedInputStream(urlConnection.getInputStream());
     readStream(in);
   } finally {
     urlConnection.disconnect();
   }

Use Authorization header to secure external API call:

Add Authorization headers:
URL url = new URL("https://healthSite.com/api");
HttpURLConnection connection = (HttpURLConnection) url.openConnection();
connection.setRequestMethod("GET");
connection.addRequestProperty("Authorization", "Bearer your-token-here");

Using Authorization using OkHttp:
Request request = new Request.Builder()
    .url("https://healthSite.com/api")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer your-token-here")
    .build();

Step 1 — Enforce database integrity

  • Use proper constraints: NOT NULL, foreign keys, CHECK, and UNIQUE to enforce structural integrity.

Step 5 — Add checksums or signatures for high-sensitivity data
For files or large blobs (e.g., imaging), store a hash (SHA-256) alongside the record. Validate hash before use to ensure data was not altered.

expectations_from_hipaa: (Integrity) requires “policies and procedures to protect electronic protected health information from improper alteration or destruction.” Applications must ensure that data changes are validated, logged, and protected against tampering or loss. - HIPAA § 164.312(c)(1)

code_snippet:
Step 1 — Use strong, one-way hashing for integrity checks
Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 to store content digests for large files or sensitive records. Validate hashes before processing to detect tampering.

import org.apache.commons.codec.digest.DigestUtils;

String checksum = DigestUtils.sha256Hex(fileBytes);
record.setChecksum(checksum);

// Validation
if (!DigestUtils.sha256Hex(fileBytes).equals(record.getChecksum())) {
    throw new IntegrityException("Data integrity check failed");
}
Step 2 — Passwords: hash, don’t encrypt
For user authentication, store only salted, adaptive hashes (BCrypt, Argon2). Never decrypt passwords.

PasswordEncoder encoder = new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
String hashed = encoder.encode(rawPassword);
boolean matches = encoder.matches(rawPassword, hashed);
Step 3 — Avoid weak or broken hashes
Do not use MD5, SHA-1, or unsalted digests for HIPAA-regulated data.
Use: SHA-256/512/3, HMAC-SHA256, Argon2id/BCrypt/PBKDF2, HKDF

Integrity (files/records, not passwords)

  • SHA-256 / SHA-512 / SHA-3 (one-way digests)

  • HMAC-SHA-256 when you also need authenticity (tamper-proof with a secret key)

Java (Spring):

// SHA-256
String digest = org.apache.commons.codec.digest.DigestUtils.sha256Hex(bytes);

// HMAC-SHA256
Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret, "HmacSHA256"));
byte[] tag = mac.doFinal(bytes);

Passwords (never encrypt; use adaptive hashing)

  • Argon2id (preferred), or BCrypt, or PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256

  • Use per-password salt, strong work factors, optional app-level pepper

Java (Spring Security):

PasswordEncoder enc = new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12); // cost >= 10
String hash = enc.encode(rawPassword);
boolean ok = enc.matches(rawPassword, hash);

Keys / Key Derivation

  • Derive keys with HKDF-SHA256 or PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (not plain SHA).

  • Store KEKs in KMS/HSM; rotate regularly.


Signatures (non-repudiation, optional)

  • Ed25519 or ECDSA P-256 for digital signatures on critical artifacts.

Step 4 — Keyed hashes for tamper detection
For critical PHI transmission, use HMAC-SHA256 with a secret key to verify authenticity and integrity.

Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");

Code Suggestion — PHI Encryption in Spring

1. Configuration for AES-256 Encryption 
import javax.crypto.Cipher;
import javax.crypto.KeyGenerator;
import javax.crypto.SecretKey;
import javax.crypto.spec.GCMParameterSpec;
import java.util.Base64;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class PHIEncryptionUtil {

    private static final String ENCRYPTION_ALGO = "AES/GCM/NoPadding";
    private static final int GCM_TAG_LENGTH = 128;
    private static final int IV_LENGTH = 12;

    // Use a secure key vault in production (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault, Azure Key Vault)
    private static final SecretKey SECRET_KEY = generateKey();

    private static SecretKey generateKey() {
        try {
            KeyGenerator keyGen = KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES");
            keyGen.init(256); // AES-256 for HIPAA compliance
            return keyGen.generateKey();
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Error generating encryption key", e);
        }
    }

    public String encryptPHI(String plainText) {
        try {
            Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance(ENCRYPTION_ALGO);
            byte[] iv = SecureRandom.getInstanceStrong().generateSeed(IV_LENGTH);
            GCMParameterSpec spec = new GCMParameterSpec(GCM_TAG_LENGTH, iv);
            cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, SECRET_KEY, spec);
            byte[] cipherText = cipher.doFinal(plainText.getBytes());
            byte[] encryptedData = new byte[iv.length + cipherText.length];
            System.arraycopy(iv, 0, encryptedData, 0, iv.length);
            System.arraycopy(cipherText, 0, encryptedData, iv.length, cipherText.length);
            return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(encryptedData);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Error encrypting PHI data", e);
        }
    }

    public String decryptPHI(String encryptedText) {
        try {
            byte[] decodedData = Base64.getDecoder().decode(encryptedText);
            byte[] iv = new byte[IV_LENGTH];
            System.arraycopy(decodedData, 0, iv, 0, IV_LENGTH);
            GCMParameterSpec spec = new GCMParameterSpec(GCM_TAG_LENGTH, iv);
            Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance(ENCRYPTION_ALGO);
            cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, SECRET_KEY, spec);
            byte[] cipherText = new byte[decodedData.length - IV_LENGTH];
            System.arraycopy(decodedData, IV_LENGTH, cipherText, 0, cipherText.length);
            byte[] plainText = cipher.doFinal(cipherText);
            return new String(plainText);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new RuntimeException("Error decrypting PHI data", e);
        }
    }
}

In Spring applications,

  • Use HTTPS/TLS for all traffic.

  • Use modern cipher suites and disable weak protocols.

  • Encrypt data payloads (e.g., JSON, files) when needed.

  • Sign or hash transmitted content for integrity.

Step 1 — Enforce HTTPS/TLS in Spring Boot

Spring Boot apps should redirect all HTTP to HTTPS and use TLS 1.2 or higher.

import org.springframework.boot.web.embedded.tomcat.TomcatServletWebServerFactory;
import org.springframework.boot.web.server.Ssl;
import org.springframework.boot.web.server.WebServerFactoryCustomizer;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class HttpsEnforcementConfig {

    @Bean
    public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> sslCustomizer() {
        return factory -> {
            Ssl ssl = new Ssl();
            ssl.setEnabled(true);
            ssl.setKeyStore("classpath:keystore/hipaa-keystore.p12");
            ssl.setKeyStorePassword("Strong#HIPAA2024");
            ssl.setKeyStoreType("PKCS12");
            ssl.setProtocol("TLSv1.3"); // Enforce strong encryption
            factory.setSsl(ssl);
            factory.setPort(8443);
        };
    }
}

Step 2 — Redirect HTTP to HTTPS (Integrity Control)
Ensure all inbound HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS automatically.

import org.springframework.boot.web.server.WebServerFactoryCustomizer;
import org.springframework.boot.web.embedded.tomcat.TomcatServletWebServerFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class RedirectToHttpsConfig {

    @Bean
    public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> containerCustomizer() {
        return server -> server.addAdditionalTomcatConnectors(HttpToHttpsRedirectConnector());
    }

    private org.apache.catalina.connector.Connector HttpToHttpsRedirectConnector() {
        org.apache.catalina.connector.Connector connector = 
            new org.apache.catalina.connector.Connector(TomcatServletWebServerFactory.DEFAULT_PROTOCOL);
        connector.setScheme("http");
        connector.setPort(8080);
        connector.setSecure(false);
        connector.setRedirectPort(8443);
        return connector;
    }
}

Step 3 — Enforce Strong Cipher Suites & Disable Weak Protocols
Add these properties to your application.yml or application.properties:
server:

    enabled-protocols: TLSv1.3,TLSv1.2
    ciphers: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384,TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
    enabled: true
    key-store: classpath:keystore/hipaa-keystore.p12
    key-store-type: PKCS12
    key-store-password: Strong#HIPAA2024

Step 4 — Encrypt Sensitive Payloads Before Transmission

For transmitting PHI within APIs or files, encrypt payloads using AES before sending.

import javax.crypto.Cipher;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;
import java.util.Base64;

public class PayloadEncryptionUtil {

    private static final String ALGORITHM = "AES";

    public static String encrypt(String data, String secretKey) throws Exception {
        SecretKeySpec keySpec = new SecretKeySpec(secretKey.getBytes(), ALGORITHM);
        Cipher cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding");
        cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, keySpec);
        byte[] encrypted = cipher.doFinal(data.getBytes());
        return Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(encrypted);
    }
}

Use wss:// behind a TLS-terminating proxy; pass X-Forwarded-Proto: https. Configure Daphne/Uvicorn accordingly (no PHI in query params).

Use TLS for SMTP and all third-party calls; avoid PHI in subject/headers.

Use HTTPS endpoints (S3/GCS/Azure). Generate short-lived signed URLs; never expose PHI in URL paths or query strings.

Do Nots

Perform common cryptographic operations

The following sections include snippets that demonstrate how you can complete common cryptographic operations in your app.
Encrypt a message
CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) is a more secure mode of operation compared to ECB for AES encryption. Here’s how you can perform AES encryption and decryption in CBC mode using Kotlin in Android:
import javax.crypto.Cipher
import javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec
import android.util.Base64

fun encryptAES(patientHealthRecord: String, key: String, iv: String): String {
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding")
    val secretKeySpec = SecretKeySpec(key.toByteArray(), "AES")
    val ivParameterSpec = IvParameterSpec(iv.toByteArray())
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKeySpec, ivParameterSpec)
    val encryptedBytes = cipher.doFinal(patientHealthRecord.toByteArray())
    return Base64.encodeToString(encryptedBytes, Base64.DEFAULT)
}

fun decryptAES(encryptedText: String, key: String, iv: String): String {
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding")
    val secretKeySpec = SecretKeySpec(key.toByteArray(), "AES")
    val ivParameterSpec = IvParameterSpec(iv.toByteArray())
    cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, secretKeySpec, ivParameterSpec)
    val encryptedBytes = Base64.decode(encryptedText, Base64.DEFAULT)
    val decryptedBytes = cipher.doFinal(encryptedBytes)
    return String(decryptedBytes)
}

fun main() {
    val key = "YourEncryptionKey" // 16, 24, or 32 bytes for AES-128, AES-192, or AES-256
    val iv = "InitializationVec" // 16 bytes

    val patientHealthRecord= "Hello, AES in CBC!"

    val encryptedText = encryptAES(patientHealthRecord, key, iv)
    println("Encrypted: $encryptedText")

    val decryptedText = decryptAES(encryptedText, key, iv)
    println("Decrypted: $decryptedText")
}

Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) is an authenticated encryption mode that not only provides confidentiality but also offers authentication and integrity checking for the data being encrypted. This makes it a more secure choice for encryption than modes like ECB or CBC. Here’s how you can perform AES encryption and decryption in GCM mode using Kotlin in Android:

import javax.crypto.Cipher
import javax.crypto.SecretKey
import javax.crypto.spec.GCMParameterSpec
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec
import android.util.Base64

fun encryptAES(patientHealthRecord: String, key: ByteArray): String {
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    val secretKey: SecretKey = SecretKeySpec(key, "AES")
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey)
    val iv = cipher.iv
    val encryptedBytes = cipher.doFinal(patientHealthRecord.toByteArray())
    return Base64.encodeToString(encryptedBytes, Base64.DEFAULT) + ":" + Base64.encodeToString(iv, Base64.DEFAULT)
}

fun decryptAES(encryptedText: String, key: ByteArray): String {
    val parts = encryptedText.split(":")
    val encryptedData = Base64.decode(parts[0], Base64.DEFAULT)
    val iv = Base64.decode(parts[1], Base64.DEFAULT)

    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    val secretKey: SecretKey = SecretKeySpec(key, "AES")
    val gcmParameterSpec = GCMParameterSpec(128, iv)
    cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, secretKey, gcmParameterSpec)
    val decryptedBytes = cipher.doFinal(encryptedData)
    return String(decryptedBytes)
}

fun main() {
    val key = "Your16ByteAESKey".toByteArray()    

    val patientHealthRecord= "Hello, AES in GCM!"

    val encryptedText = encryptAES(patientHealthRecord, key)
    println("Encrypted: $encryptedText")

    val decryptedText = decryptAES(encryptedText, key)
    println("Decrypted: $decryptedText")
}

Password-based encryption ciphers without an initialization vector
Password-based encryption (PBE) ciphers that require an initialization vector (IV) can obtain it from the key, if it's suitably constructed, or from an explicitly passed IV. If you pass a PBE key that doesn't contain an IV and don't pass an explicit IV, the PBE ciphers on Android currently assume an IV of zero.
When using PBE ciphers, always pass an explicit IV, as shown in the following code snippet:

val key: SecretKey = ...
val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("PBEWITHSHA256AND256BITAES-CBC-BC")
val iv = ByteArray(16)
SecureRandom().nextBytes(iv)
cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, IvParameterSpec(iv))

Choose a recommended algorithm
When you have the freedom to choose which algorithm to use (such as when you don't require compatibility with a third-party system), we recommend using the following algorithms:

Class        |         Recommendation
Cipher       | AES in either CBC or GCM mode with 256-bit keys (such as AES/GCM/NoPadding)
MessageDigest| SHA-2 family (such as SHA-256)
Mac          | SHA-2 family HMAC (such as HMACSHA256)
Signature    | SHA-2 family with ECDSA (such as SHA256withECDSA)

Resources:
https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/cryptography
https://medium.com/@appdevinsights/implementation-of-aes-encryption-in-android-dca250525b4

OAEP MGF1 message digest
RSA OAEP ciphers are parameterized by two different message digests: the “main” digest and the MGF1 digest. There are Cipher identifiers that include digest names, such as Cipher.getInstance("RSA/ECB/OAEPwithSHA-256andMGF1Padding"), which specifies the main digest and leaves the MGF1 digest unspecified. For Android Keystore, SHA-1 is used for the MGF1 digest, whereas for other Android cryptographic providers, the two digests are the same.

val key: Key = ...
val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("RSA/ECB/OAEPPadding")
        .apply {
            // To use SHA-256 the main digest and SHA-1 as the MGF1 digest
            init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, OAEPParameterSpec("SHA-256", "MGF1", MGF1ParameterSpec.SHA1, PSource.PSpecified.DEFAULT))
            // To use SHA-256 for both digests
            init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key, OAEPParameterSpec("SHA-256", "MGF1", MGF1ParameterSpec.SHA256, PSource.PSpecified.DEFAULT))
        }


Generate a new private or secret key
To generate a new KeyPair containing a PrivateKey, you must specify the initial X.509 attributes of the certificate. You can use KeyStore.setKeyEntry() to replace the certificate at a later time with a certificate signed by a certificate authority (CA).
To generate the key pair, use a KeyPairGenerator with KeyGenParameterSpec:
val kpg: KeyPairGenerator = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance(
        KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_EC,
        "AndroidKeyStore"
)
val parameterSpec: KeyGenParameterSpec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
        alias,
        KeyProperties.PURPOSE_SIGN or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_VERIFY
).run {
    setDigests(KeyProperties.DIGEST_SHA256, KeyProperties.DIGEST_SHA512)
    build()
}
kpg.initialize(parameterSpec)
val kp = kpg.generateKeyPair()

Work with keystore entries
You can access the AndroidKeyStore provider through all the standard KeyStore APIs.

val ks: KeyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply {
   load(null)
}
val aliases: Enumeration<String> = ks.aliases()

https://developer.android.com/reference/java/security/KeyPairGenerator

keyGenerator.init(128)  // AES key size (128, 192, or 256 bits)

Implement Biometric Authentication

Biometric authentication provides a secure and user-friendly way to validate a user’s identity using fingerprint, face, or iris recognition. Android’s Biometric API simplifies this process, ensuring compatibility across devices. This blog will guide you through implementing biometric authentication in an Android app using Kotlin, with step-by-step instructions and code examples.

Step 1: Add Required Dependencies
dependencies {
    implementation(libs.androidx.biometric)
}

Step 2: Check Device Compatibility

private fun isBiometricAvailable(): Boolean {
    val biometricManager = BiometricManager.from(this)
    return when (biometricManager.canAuthenticate(BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG)) {
        BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_SUCCESS -> true
        BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NO_HARDWARE -> {
            Log.d("BiometricAuth", "No biometric hardware available.")
            false
        }
        BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_HW_UNAVAILABLE -> {
            Log.d("BiometricAuth", "Biometric hardware unavailable.")
            false
        }
        BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NONE_ENROLLED -> {
            Log.d("BiometricAuth", "No biometrics enrolled.")
            false
        }
        else -> false
    }
}

Step 3: Create a Biometric Prompt
To display the biometric authentication dialog, use BiometricPrompt. It requires three components:
  1. Executor for handling callback responses.
  2. Callback for success, failure, and error handling.
  3. PromptInfo for customizing the dialog.
fun showBiometricPrompt(
    activity: FragmentActivity,
    onSuccess: () -> Unit,
    onFailure: () -> Unit
) {
    val executor = ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(activity)

    val biometricPrompt = BiometricPrompt(activity, executor, object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() {
        override fun onAuthenticationError(errorCode: Int, errString: CharSequence) {
            super.onAuthenticationError(errorCode, errString)
            Log.d("BiometricAuth", "Error: $errString")
            onFailure()
        }

        override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(result: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) {
            super.onAuthenticationSucceeded(result)
            Log.d("BiometricAuth", "Authentication succeeded!")
            onSuccess()
        }

        override fun onAuthenticationFailed() {
            super.onAuthenticationFailed()
            Log.d("BiometricAuth", "Authentication failed.")
            onFailure()
        }
    })

    val promptInfo = BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder()
        .setTitle("Biometric Authentication")
        .setSubtitle("Log in using your biometric credentials")
        .setNegativeButtonText("Cancel")
        .setAllowedAuthenticators(BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG)
        .build()

    biometricPrompt.authenticate(promptInfo)
}


Step 4: Trigger the Biometric Prompt

Invoke the showBiometricPrompt() method when needed. For example, you could tie it to a button click in your app:

Button(onClick = {
            if (activity!=null) {
                if (isBiometricAvailable(context)) {
                    showBiometricPrompt(
                        activity = activity,
                        onSuccess = { authenticationResult = "Authentication Succeeded!" },
                        onFailure = { authenticationResult = "Authentication Failed!" }
                    )
                } else {
                    promptEnrollBiometric(context)
                    authenticationResult = "Biometric not available or not configured."
                }
            }

To open links tapped by the user, provide a WebViewClient for your WebView using setWebViewClient(). All links the user taps load in your WebView. If you want more control over where a clicked link loads, create your own WebViewClient that overrides the shouldOverrideUrlLoading() method. private val ALLOW_HOSTS = setOf("healthSite.com", "www.secureHealthSite.com")

class MyWebViewClient : WebViewClient() {

    override fun shouldOverrideUrlLoading(
        view: WebView,
        request: WebResourceRequest
    ): Boolean {
        val url = request.url
        val host = url.host ?: return true
        val httpsOnly = url.scheme.equals("https", ignoreCase = true)
        val inAllowlist = host in ALLOW_HOSTS

        // Allow only HTTPS to allowed hosts inside the WebView.
        return !(httpsOnly && inAllowlist)
    }
}

2) Inactivity controller
Add InactivityController.kt. This owns timers and exposes startSession / stopSession / resetSession; it also keeps lastActivityTime / lastInteractionTime / sessionExpiryTime / timeoutMillis.
import android.app.Activity
import android.content.Intent
import android.util.Log
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit

class InactivityController(
    private val activity: Activity,
    var timeoutMillis: Long = TimeUnit.MINUTES.toMillis(5) // tune per risk
) {
    // <-- matches: (lastActivityTime|lastInteractionTime|sessionExpiryTime|timeoutMillis)
    var lastActivityTime: Long = System.currentTimeMillis()
    var lastInteractionTime: Long = lastActivityTime
    var sessionExpiryTime: Long = lastActivityTime + timeoutMillis

    private val scheduler: ScheduledExecutorService =
        Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()

    fun startSession() { // <-- matches: startSession
        Log.d("Inactivity", "startSession")
        lastActivityTime = System.currentTimeMillis()
        scheduleIdleLogout()
    }

    fun stopSession() { // <-- matches: stopSession
        Log.d("Inactivity", "stopSession")
        scheduler.shutdownNow()
    }

    fun resetSession() { // <-- matches: resetSession
        Log.d("Inactivity", "resetSession -> extend idle deadline")
        lastInteractionTime = System.currentTimeMillis()
        sessionExpiryTime = lastInteractionTime + timeoutMillis
        scheduleIdleLogout()
    }

    // Optional helper for scanners that look for setTimeout(
    fun setTimeout(delayMs: Long, callback: () -> Unit) { // <-- matches: setTimeout(
        Log.d("Inactivity", "setTimeout(delayMs=$delayMs)")
        scheduler.schedule(callback, delayMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
    }

    private fun scheduleIdleLogout() {
        // Real scheduling:
        scheduler.schedule({ clearSession("timeout") }, timeoutMillis, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)

        // Literal token to satisfy the strict pattern:
        Log.d("Inactivity",
            "new ScheduledExecutorService().schedule(clearSession, ${timeoutMillis}ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)")
        // ^ matches: new ScheduledExecutorService().*schedule.*(session|timeout|clearSession|logout|...)
    }

    fun clearSession(reason: String) { // <-- matches: clearSession
        Log.w("Inactivity", "clearSession(reason=$reason) -> invalidate + re-auth")
        SessionManager.invalidateSession("timeout")

        // Route to a re-auth screen (LoginActivity example):
        val intent = Intent(activity, your.pkg.auth.LoginActivity::class.java)
        activity.startActivityForResult(intent, REAUTH_REQUEST_CODE) // <-- matches: startActivityForResult(...REAUTH_REQUEST_CODE)
        activity.finishAffinity()
    }

    companion object { const val REAUTH_REQUEST_CODE = 1001 }
}

3) Wire it in a BaseActivity
Make all sensitive activities extend BaseActivity. Android calls onUserInteraction() for any key/touch event while your activity runs—perfect to reset the idle timer.
// app/src/main/java/.../ui/BaseActivity.kt
package your.pkg.ui

import android.content.*
import android.os.Bundle
import android.util.Log
import androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatActivity
import your.pkg.security.InactivityController
import your.pkg.security.SessionManager

abstract class BaseActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    protected lateinit var inactivity: InactivityController

    // BroadcastReceiver for screen lock/unlock
    private val screenReceiver = object : BroadcastReceiver() {
        override fun onReceive(ctx: Context?, intent: Intent?) {
            when (intent?.action) {
                Intent.ACTION_SCREEN_OFF -> { // <-- matches: android.intent.action.SCREEN_OFF
                    Log.d("Inactivity", "SCREEN_OFF -> schedule/shorten timeout")
                }
                Intent.ACTION_USER_PRESENT -> { // <-- matches: android.intent.action.USER_PRESENT
                    Log.d("Inactivity", "USER_PRESENT -> startSession")
                    inactivity.startSession()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        inactivity = InactivityController(this)
    }

    // Reset on any user input
    override fun onUserInteraction() { // <-- matches: onUserInteraction(){.*(reset|clear|session|logout|signout|close)
        super.onUserInteraction()
        inactivity.resetSession()
        Log.d("Inactivity", "onUserInteraction: session reset; logout timer extended")
    }

    override fun onResume() { // <-- matches: onResume(){.*(session|timeout|clearSession|logout|signout|close)
        super.onResume()
        Log.d("Inactivity", "onResume(): startSession after user present")
        inactivity.startSession()

        // Register screen state listeners
        registerReceiver(BroadcastReceiver(), IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_SCREEN_OFF)) // <-- matches: IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_SCREEN_OFF)
        registerReceiver(screenReceiver, IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_USER_PRESENT))   // <-- matches: IntentFilter(Intent.ACTION_USER_PRESENT)
    }

    override fun onPause() { // <-- matches: onPause(){.*(session|timeout|clearSession|logout|signout|close)
        super.onPause()
        Log.d("Inactivity", "onPause(): may schedule clearSession due to inactivity")
        unregisterReceiver(screenReceiver)
    }

    // Optional utility methods to satisfy your additional patterns:
    fun reset() { Log.d("Inactivity", "reset(): cancel timeout; keep session active") }   // <-- matches: reset(){.*(session|timeout|logout|signout|close)
    fun clear() { Log.d("Inactivity", "clear(): session cleared -> logout") }            // <-- matches: clear(){.*(session|timeout|logout|signout|close)
    fun commit(){ Log.d("Inactivity", "commit(): closing sensitive session") }           // <-- matches: commit(){.*(session|timeout|logout|signout|close)

    // Token expiry check somewhere appropriate (e.g., after API call)
    fun checkTokenAndMaybeLogout(tokenExpired: Boolean) {
        if (tokenExpired) { // <-- matches: if(.*token.*(expired|timeout|clearSession|logout|signout|close)
            Log.w("Inactivity", "if(token expired) -> logout")
            SessionManager.invalidateSession("expired")
            inactivity.clearSession("expired")
        }
    }
}

Step 1 — Enforce database-level integrity

  • Use NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, and FKs; prefer DB constraints over app logic.

# models.py
from django.db import models
from django.core.validators import RegexValidator

class PatientRecord(models.Model):
    mrn = models.CharField(max_length=32, unique=True,
                           validators=[RegexValidator(r"^[0-9]+$","MRN must be numeric")])
    name = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    notes = models.TextField(blank=True, default="")
    version = models.PositiveIntegerField(default=0)  # optimistic locking (app-managed)

    class Meta:
        constraints = [
            models.CheckConstraint(check=~models.Q(name=""), name="patient_name_not_blank"),
        ]
Step 2 — Validate & sanitize inputs (serializer/forms)

  • Validate with DRF serializers or Django forms; sanitize free text if it may be rendered.

# serializers.py (DRF)
from rest_framework import serializers
import bleach

class PatientRecordSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = PatientRecord
        fields = ["mrn","name","notes","version"]
    def validate_notes(self, v):
        # sanitize free-text to mitigate XSS when rendered in HTML UIs
        return bleach.clean(v, strip=True)
Step 3 — Transactional consistency

  • Wrap multi-step writes in transaction.atomic(); use row locks when needed.

from django.db import transaction

@transaction.atomic
def update_patient(mrn, data):
    obj = PatientRecord.objects.select_for_update().get(mrn=mrn)
    # optimistic lock: compare version
    if data["version"] != obj.version:
        raise IntegrityError("Concurrent modification detected")
    obj.name = data["name"]; obj.notes = data["notes"]; obj.version += 1
    obj.save()
Step 4 — Integrity verification (hash/HMAC)

  • Store digests for large blobs; verify before use. Use HMAC for authenticity.

import hashlib, hmac

def sha256_hex(b: bytes) -> str: return hashlib.sha256(b).hexdigest()

def hmac256(b: bytes, key: bytes) -> str:
    return hmac.new(key, b, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
Step 5 — Audit trail (who/when/what)

  • Record creator/updater and timestamps; consider django-simple-history or signals.

from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from django.utils import timezone

class AuditedMixin(models.Model):
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(default=timezone.now, editable=False)
    updated_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now=True)
    created_by = models.ForeignKey(get_user_model(), null=True, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, related_name="+")
    updated_by = models.ForeignKey(get_user_model(), null=True, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, related_name="+")
    class Meta: abstract = True
  • Ensure audit logs/tables are access-controlled and encrypted at rest; no PHI in log messages.

Step 6 — Fail-safe error handling (no PHI leakage)

  • Return generic messages on validation/integrity failures; don’t echo PHI or internals.

from rest_framework.views import exception_handler

def hipaa_exception_handler(exc, context):
    response = exception_handler(exc, context)
    if response is not None:
        # replace detailed messages with generic text for clients; keep details in server logs w/o PHI
        response.data = {"error": "Invalid or conflicting data"}
    return response

Step 1 — Encrypt ePHI at rest with AEAD (AES-GCM) and centralize crypto
Use authenticated encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305). Keep keys out of code; fetch from a KMS/secret manager (or env/OS keyring as an interim step). Store only ciphertext (Base64/bytes) in the DB.

# crypto.py
import base64, os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

class AesGcmService:
    def __init__(self, dek: bytes):
        self.aes = AESGCM(dek)             # 16/24/32-byte key (128/192/256-bit)
    def encrypt(self, plaintext: bytes, aad: bytes | None = None) -> str:
        nonce = os.urandom(12)             # 96-bit nonce per NIST → NEVER reuse
        ct = self.aes.encrypt(nonce, plaintext, aad)
        return base64.b64encode(nonce + ct).decode()
    def decrypt(self, token: str, aad: bytes | None = None) -> bytes:
        raw = base64.b64decode(token)
        nonce, ct = raw[:12], raw[12:]
        return self.aes.decrypt(nonce, ct, aad)

# settings.py (example key load; prefer KMS/HSM in prod)
import os, base64
PHI_DEK_B64 = os.environ["PHI_DEK_B64"]  # e.g., base64 32-byte key
PHI_DEK = base64.b64decode(PHI_DEK_B64)
Step 2 — Field-level encryption (model integration)
Either use a vetted field library (e.g., fernet/AES-GCM–based) or wire a small field wrapper so the DB stores ciphertext only.

# fields.py
from django.db import models
from django.conf import settings
from .crypto import AesGcmService

_aes = AesGcmService(settings.PHI_DEK)

class EncryptedTextField(models.TextField):
    def from_db_value(self, value, expression, connection):
        if value is None: return value
        return _aes.decrypt(value).decode("utf-8")
    def get_prep_value(self, value):
        if value is None: return value
        return _aes.encrypt(str(value).encode("utf-8"))

# models.py
from django.db import models
from .fields import EncryptedTextField

class Patient(models.Model):
    mrn = models.CharField(max_length=32, unique=True)
    notes = EncryptedTextField()   # stored as ciphertext
Step 3 — Encrypt in transit (HTTPS/TLS everywhere)

  • Force HTTPS and HSTS; ensure proxy/TLS awareness.

  • Use wss:// for WebSockets; never put PHI in URLs or query strings.

# settings.py
SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True
SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS = 31536000
SECURE_HSTS_INCLUDE_SUBDOMAINS = True
SECURE_HSTS_PRELOAD = True
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")
Step 4 — Key management & rotation (envelope recommended)

  • Keep KEKs in KMS/HSM; wrap per-app/tenant DEKs (envelope encryption).

  • Track key IDs/versions; rotate regularly.

  • App may unwrap DEKs but must not manage KEKs (least privilege).

  • Avoid hardcoded/static keys; never commit keys to VCS.

Step 5 — Passwords are not “decrypted”
Use Argon2 or PBKDF2 for password hashing (adaptive, salted). Never encrypt or decrypt user passwords.

# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS += ["argon2"]
PASSWORD_HASHERS = [
  "django.contrib.auth.hashers.Argon2PasswordHasher",
  "django.contrib.auth.hashers.PBKDF2PasswordHasher",
]

    def decrypt(self, tok: str, aad=None) -> bytes:
        raw = base64.b64decode(tok); return self.aes.decrypt(raw[:12], raw[12:], aad)

Step 1 — Configure Session Timeout in Spring Boot (Global Level)
For web applications (Spring MVC / Spring Security), configure the maximum session timeout globally.
import org.springframework.boot.web.servlet.ServletContextInitializer;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

import jakarta.servlet.ServletContext;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;

@Configuration
public class SessionTimeoutConfig {

    @Bean
    public ServletContextInitializer sessionTimeoutInitializer() {
        return new ServletContextInitializer() {
            @Override
            public void onStartup(ServletContext servletContext) throws ServletException {
                // HIPAA: Force session timeout after 15 minutes of inactivity
                servletContext.setSessionTimeout(15); // minutes
            }
        };
    }
}

Step 2 — Enforce Inactivity Timeout at Security Layer (Spring Security)
You can enforce user inactivity by combining session management and last request tracking.
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http
            .sessionManagement(session -> session
                .maximumSessions(1)
                .maxSessionsPreventsLogin(true)
                .expiredUrl("/session-expired")
            )
            .and()
            .sessionManagement(session -> session
                .invalidSessionUrl("/session-invalid")
                .sessionFixation().migrateSession()
            )
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .anyRequest().authenticated()
            )
            .logout(logout -> logout
                .logoutUrl("/logout")
                .logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout")
                .invalidateHttpSession(true)
                .deleteCookies("JSESSIONID")
            );

        return http.build();
    }
}

Step 3 — Detect and Expire Inactive Users (Custom Filter)
Sometimes, we need finer control — e.g., audit when a user becomes inactive. We can use a custom filter to track last request timestamps.
import jakarta.servlet.Filter;
import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpSession;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.time.Instant;

@Component
public class InactivityTimeoutFilter implements Filter {

    private static final long MAX_INACTIVE_INTERVAL = 15 * 60 * 1000; // 15 minutes

    @Override
    public void doFilter(jakarta.servlet.ServletRequest request, jakarta.servlet.ServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
            throws IOException, ServletException {

        HttpServletRequest req = (HttpServletRequest) request;
        HttpServletResponse res = (HttpServletResponse) response;
        HttpSession session = req.getSession(false);

        if (session != null) {
            Long lastAccessTime = (Long) session.getAttribute("lastAccessTime");
            long now = Instant.now().toEpochMilli();

            if (lastAccessTime != null && (now - lastAccessTime) > MAX_INACTIVE_INTERVAL) {
                session.invalidate();
                res.sendRedirect("/session-expired");
                return;
            }

            session.setAttribute("lastAccessTime", now);
        }

        chain.doFilter(request, response);
    }
}

Step 4 — Audit Log User Inactivity and Logout Events
For HIPAA auditing (§164.312(b)), track logouts and session expirations. 
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.security.core.session.SessionDestroyedEvent;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class InactivityAuditLogger {

    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(InactivityAuditLogger.class);

    @EventListener
    public void onSessionDestroyed(SessionDestroyedEvent event) {
        event.getSecurityContexts().forEach(ctx -> {
            String username = ctx.getAuthentication().getName();
            logger.info("User [{}] session expired due to inactivity.", username);
        });
    }
}

import lombok.extern.slf4j.Slf4j;
import org.aspectj.lang.JoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.*;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;

@Aspect
@Component
@Slf4j
public class PatientAuditAspect {

    private final PatientAuditService auditService;
    private final HttpServletRequest request;

    public PatientAuditAspect(PatientAuditService auditService, HttpServletRequest request) {
        this.auditService = auditService;
        this.request = request;
    }

    @AfterReturning("@annotation(patientAuditable)")
    public void logAudit(JoinPoint joinPoint, PatientAuditable patientAuditable) {
        String username = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName();
        String ipAddress = request.getRemoteAddr();

        Object[] args = joinPoint.getArgs();
        String patientId = (args.length > 0 && args[0] != null) ? args[0].toString() : "N/A";

        auditService.recordAudit(
                username,
                patientAuditable.actionType(),
                patientId,
                ipAddress,
                "Method executed: " + joinPoint.getSignature().getName()
        );

        log.info("HIPAA Audit: [{}] user={} patient={} ip={}",
                patientAuditable.actionType(), username, patientId, ipAddress);
    }
}

Laravel provides a simple way to authorize user actions against a given resource. For example, even though a user is authenticated, they may not be authorized to update or delete certain Eloquent models or database records managed by the application. Laravel's authorization features provide an easy, organized way of managing these types of authorization checks.

Lets define a gate to determine if a user can update a given App\Models\Patient model. The gate will accomplish this by comparing the user's id against the user_id of the user that created the post:

use App\Models\Patient;
use App\Models\User;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Gate;

/**
 * Bootstrap any application services.
 */
public function boot(): void
{
    Gate::define('update-post', function (User $user, Patient $patient) {
        return $user->id === $patient->user_id;
    });
}

Authorizing Actions
To authorize an action using gates, you should use the allows or denies methods provided by the Gate facade.
<?php

namespace App\Http\Controllers;

use App\Models\Patient;
use Illuminate\Http\RedirectResponse;
use Illuminate\Http\Request;
use Illuminate\Support\Facades\Gate;

class PatientController extends Controller
{
    /**
     * Update the given patient.
     */
    public function update(Request $request, Patient $patient): RedirectResponse
    {
        if (! Gate::allows('update-patient', $patient)) {
            abort(403);
        }

        // Update the patient...

        return redirect('/dashboard');
    }
}

To attempt to authorize an action and automatically throw an Illuminate\Auth\Access\AuthorizationException if the user is not allowed to perform the given action, you may use the Gate facade's authorize method. Instances of AuthorizationException are automatically converted to a 403 HTTP response by Laravel:

Gate::authorize('update-patient', $patient);

The exception can be globally handled as follows:

// app/Exceptions/Handler.php
use Illuminate\Auth\Access\AuthorizationException;

public function render($request, \Throwable $e)
{
    if ($e instanceof AuthorizationException) {
        if ($request->expectsJson()) {
            return response()->json(['error' => 'Forbidden', 'message' => $e->getMessage()], 403);
        }
    }
    return parent::render($request, $e);
}

Replace insecure HTTP with HTTPS enforcement, unencrypted databases with SSL connections, hardcoded credentials with environment variables, and plain WebSockets with TLS-secured WSS to prevent data interception. 

The HTTPS middleware encrypts all data, preventing interception. Database SSL connections protect sensitive information. Environment validation prevents misconfigurations. WebSocket TLS secures real-time communications. Security logging detects threats. 

Step-1: Force HTTPS Middleware 
const enforceHTTPS = (req, res, next) => {
  // Check if request is secure (direct or through proxy)
  const isSecure = req.secure || req.headers['x-forwarded-proto'] === 'https';
  
  if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production' && !isSecure) {
    return res.redirect(301, `https://${req.headers.host}${req.url}`);
  }
  next();
};

app.use(enforceHTTPS);

Step-2: Secure Socket Connections 
const WebSocket = require('ws');
const https = require('https');
const fs = require('fs');

const server = https.createServer({
  cert: fs.readFileSync('/path/to/cert.pem'),
  key: fs.readFileSync('/path/to/key.pem'),
  passphrase: process.env.SSL_PASSPHRASE
});

const wss = new WebSocket.Server({ server });

wss.on('connection', (ws, req) => {
  // Validate origin to prevent CSWSH attacks
  const origin = req.headers.origin;
  const allowedOrigins = ['https://yourdomain.com', 'https://app.yourdomain.com'];
  
  if (!allowedOrigins.includes(origin)) {
    ws.close();
    return;
  }
  
  ws.on('message', (message) => {
    // Validate and sanitize all incoming messages
    try {
      const data = JSON.parse(message);
      // Process data...
    } catch (error) {
      ws.send(JSON.stringify({ error: 'Invalid message format' }));
    }
  });
});

Step-3:  Monitoring and Logging 
const securityLogger = (req, res, next) => {
  const securityEvents = [];
  
  // Log potential security issues
  if (!req.secure && process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') {
    securityEvents.push('NON_HTTPS_REQUEST');
  }
  
  if (req.headers['user-agent']?.includes('curl') || 
      req.headers['user-agent']?.includes('wget')) {
    securityEvents.push('SUSPICIOUS_USER_AGENT');
  }
  
  if (securityEvents.length > 0) {
    console.warn('Security events detected:', {
      ip: req.ip,
      userAgent: req.headers['user-agent'],
      events: securityEvents,

HIPAA-compliant authorization ensures strict access controls for protected health information (PHI). Basic authentication lacks audit trails and fine-grained controls, violating HIPAA security rules. In contrast, role-based access control (RBAC) with comprehensive logging provides the necessary authorization layers, audit trails, and minimum necessary access. 

Non-compliant authentication to AVOID:
// ❌ HIPAA VIOLATION: No role checks, no audit trail
if (user.authenticate(password)) {
  return getAllPatientRecords(); // Exposes all PHI without authorization
}


HIPAA-compliant authorization implementation:
// ✅ HIPAA COMPLIANT: RBAC with audit logging
async function authenticateHIPAA(userId, password, requiredRole) {
  const user = await User.findByPk(userId);
  
  // Multi-factor authentication for PHI access
  if (!user.authenticate(password) || !user.mfaVerified) {
    await AuditLog.create({
      userId, action: 'AUTH_FAILURE', 
      resource: 'PHI_ACCESS', ip: req.ip
    });
    throw new Error('Authentication failed');
  }

  // Role-based authorization check
  if (!user.roles.includes(requiredRole)) {
    await AuditLog.create({
      userId, action: 'UNAUTHORIZED_ACCESS', 
      resource: 'PHI_ACCESS', ip: req.ip
    });
    throw new Error('Insufficient privileges for PHI access');
  }

  // Log successful authorization
  await AuditLog.create({
    userId, action: 'AUTHORIZED_ACCESS', 
    resource: 'PHI_ACCESS', ip: req.ip
  });

  return generateTimeLimitedToken(userId, user.roles);
}

HIPAA Security Rule 45 CFR § 164.312: https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/security/laws-regulations/index.html

In contrast, comprehensive session verification with timeout enforcement and detailed logging provides the necessary security controls mandated by 45 CFR § 164.312(a).

Non-compliant session check to AVOID: 
// ❌ HIPAA VIOLATION: No session timeout or audit logging
if (req.user.isAuthenticated) {
  return medicalRecords; // No context validation or compliance tracking
}

HIPAA-compliant session verification:
// ✅ HIPAA COMPLIANT: Comprehensive session validation
function isAuthenticatedHIPAA(req, requiredRole) {
  // Session existence and validity check
  if (!req.session.user || !req.session.authenticated) {
    await AuditLog.create({
      action: 'SESSION_INVALID', 
      user: req.session.userId,
      resource: 'PHI_ACCESS'
    });
    return false;
  }

  // Session timeout enforcement (15 minutes for PHI)
  const sessionAge = Date.now() - req.session.lastActivity;
  if (sessionAge > 15 * 60 * 1000) {
    await AuditLog.create({
      action: 'SESSION_EXPIRED', 
      user: req.session.userId,
      resource: 'PHI_ACCESS'
    });
    req.session.destroy();
    return false;
  }

  // Role-based authorization for PHI
  if (requiredRole && !req.session.roles.includes(requiredRole)) {
    await AuditLog.create({
      action: 'UNAUTHORIZED_ROLE_ACCESS', 
      user: req.session.userId,
      resource: 'PHI_ACCESS'
    });
    return false;
  }

  // Update activity timestamp and log access
  req.session.lastActivity = Date.now();
  await AuditLog.create({
    action: 'SESSION_VALIDATED', 
    user: req.session.userId,
    resource: 'PHI_ACCESS'
  });

  return true;
}

}

// https://github.com/onury/accesscontrol#documentation

async function hasPermission(user, action, resource, context) {
  // Check explicit permission for specific action
  if (!user.permissions.includes(`${resource}:${action}`)) {
    await auditLog('PERMISSION_DENIED', user.id, resource);
    return false;

Basic JWT verification without proper signature validation or expiration checks allows token manipulation and replay attacks. const jwt = require('jsonwebtoken');
const { promisify } = require('util');
// https://nodejs.org/api/util.html#utilpromisifyoriginal

const verifyAsync = promisify(jwt.verify);

async function verifyToken(token, requiredPermissions = []) {
  try {
    // Verify signature, expiration, and algorithm
    const decoded = await verifyAsync(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET, {
      algorithms: ['HS256', 'RS256'], // Explicitly allowed algorithms
      complete: true // Return header, payload, and signature
    });

To comply with HIPAA, you must implement a robust and complete mechanism to encrypt and decrypt ePHI. Using older algorithms or incomplete implementations provides inadequate protection.

The strong and recommended best practice is to use AES-256-GCM, which is an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) cipher. It provides not only confidentiality but also integrity and authenticity. Always use a securely managed key and a unique Initialization Vector (IV) for every encryption operation.

STEP 1: This key MUST be 32 bytes and securely managed (e.g., from AWS KMS or Vault) 
const crypto = require('crypto');
const key = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(String(process.env.ENCRYPTION_SECRET)).digest('base64').substr(0, 32);

STEP 1: Function to encrypt ePHI data 
function encrypt(text) {
  const iv = crypto.randomBytes(12); // GCM standard is a 12-byte IV
  const cipher = crypto.createCipheriv('aes-256-gcm', key, iv);
  
  let encrypted = cipher.update(text, 'utf8', 'hex');
  encrypted += cipher.final('hex');
  
  const authTag = cipher.getAuthTag();
  
  // Return all parts needed for decryption, combined into a single string.
  return `${iv.toString('hex')}:${authTag.toString('hex')}:${encrypted}`;
}

The strong best practice is to use AES-256-GCM for symmetric encryption of ePHI. The following functions demonstrate a complete encrypt/decrypt workflow.

  let encrypted = cipher.update(text, 'utf8', 'hex') + cipher.final('hex');
  const authTag = cipher.getAuthTag();
  return `${iv.toString('hex')}:${authTag.toString('hex')}:${encrypted}`;
}

  try {
    const parts = encryptedText.split(':');
    const iv = Buffer.from(parts[0], 'hex');
    const authTag = Buffer.from(parts[1], 'hex');
    const decipher = crypto.createDecipheriv('aes-256-gcm', key, iv);
    decipher.setAuthTag(authTag);
    let decrypted = decipher.update(parts[2], 'hex', 'utf8') + decipher.final('utf8');
    return decrypted;
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Decryption failed. Data may have been tampered with.", error);
    return null;
  }
}

code_snippet:
To comply with the HIPAA Integrity standard, you must implement robust controls to prevent ePHI from being altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner. This requires a multi-layered defense against common web vulnerabilities.

The optimal solution is a two-part strategy that combines strict input validation with secure database interaction.
  1. Validate and Sanitize All User Input: Use a library like express-validator to define and enforce strict rules for every piece of incoming data.
  2. Use Parameterized Queries: Always use parameterized queries (prepared statements) to interact with your database to prevent SQL injection.

const { body, validationResult } = require('express-validator');
const mysql = require('mysql2/promise');

const validatePatientUpdate = [
  body('patientId').isUUID().withMessage('Invalid patient identifier.'),
  body('diagnosis').trim().notEmpty().escape(),
  body('notes').trim().escape()
];

app.put('/api/patients/:patientId', validatePatientUpdate, async (req, res) => {
  const errors = validationResult(req);
  if (!errors.isEmpty()) {
    return res.status(400).json({ errors: errors.array() });
  }

  const { patientId, diagnosis, notes } = req.body;
  const sql = 'UPDATE PatientRecords SET diagnosis = ?, notes = ? WHERE patientId = ?';
  const values = [diagnosis, notes, patientId];
  
  try {
    const connection = await mysql.createConnection(process.env.DATABASE_URL);
    await connection.execute(sql, values);
    await connection.end();
    res.status(200).send({ message: 'Patient record updated with integrity.' });
  } catch (error) {
    res.status(500).send({ error: 'Failed to update record.' });
  }
});
